ABSTRACT
Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) have garnered significant attention as artificial synapses due to their ability to
emulate synaptic functionalities. While previous research has predominantly focused on modulating the physical properties of
the channel materials to enhance synaptic performance, the role of ion dynamics in influencing device characteristics remains
underexplored. Effective regulation of ion dynamics is crucial for improving state retention and achieving long‐term plasticity
(LTP) in these devices. In this study, we propose a strategy to modulate the interactions between polymer semiconductors and
ions in solid‐electrolyte‐based artificial synapses. Our findings indicate that the interplay between semiconductors and doping
counterions significantly influences ion transport dynamics, thereby affecting the electrochemical doping and dedoping pro-
cesses in OECTs. Notably, by suppressing the dedoping process, we achieved enhanced synaptic performances, with devices
retaining 64% of the peak current after a retention time of 1000 s. Through the judicious selection of anions and optimization of
their interactions with polymer semiconductors, we effectively controlled the dedoping process in OECTs, leading to improved
state retention. These insights provide a novel perspective on tuning ion‐polymer semiconductor interactions for the
development of high‐performance synaptic devices, advancing neuromorphic computing applications.

Introduction
Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) have emerged as
ideal candidates for constructing artificial synapses [1], owing
to their high conductance [2], low power consumption [3, 4],
easy
fabrication
[5],
low
operating
voltage
[6,
7],
and
biocompatibility [8]. These features have facilitated their
widespread application in various fields, including bioelec-
tronics [9, 10], wearable electronics [11], and neuromorphic
electronics [12]. Neuromorphic computing technology achieves
outstanding parallel and information processing capabilities by
simulating the synaptic plasticity of biological neurons. Within

this framework, artificial synapses serve as integral components
of neural networks, enabling the transmission and modulation
of signals [13–15]. The primary functions of artificial synapses
encompass excitatory postsynaptic current (EPSC), short‐term
plasticity (STP), and long‐term plasticity (LTP) [16]. Notably,
LTP is the basis of long‐term memory function, and state
retention is a manifestation of simulating LTP by OECTs, which
is critical for neuromorphic computing applications, such as
image recognition or data storage [17]. OECTs achieve the
simulation of synaptic functions through ion doping and de-
doping mechanisms [8]. However, the rapid dedoping of ions
significantly reduces the synaptic retention time of the devices,
which not only hinders the realization of LTP, but also limits
their applications in neuromorphic computing. Therefore,
developing devices with excellent state retention is crucial for
improving the accuracy of image recognition applications [18].
Currently, research addressing the issue of rapid dedoping pri-
marily focuses on two approaches to enhance device performance:
optimizing the intrinsic properties of semiconductors or refining
fabrication processes. In terms of material modification, Sung et al.
[19] employed a copolymerization method, achieving retention
rate of approximately 25% and significantly improving the state
retention of the devices. Furthermore, modifying the length of
side‐chain alkyl spacer [20] or inducing phase separation within
the channel layer to form micropores [21] can also delay ion back‐
diffusion and enhance the synaptic performance of the devices.
Regarding process optimization, solvent engineering [22] or
blending methods have been shown to improve the retention ratio
by approximately threefold, effectively modulating the synaptic
plasticity of devices [23]. However, these approaches encounter
several challenges. On one hand, they may complicate the syn-
thesis process and necessitate precise control over solvent selection
and processing conditions. On the other hand, while slowing
down the dedoping process, these methods may simultaneously
weaken the electrochemical doping process of the devices.
The operation of OECTs is governed by the coupling effect
between ions in the electrolyte and electrons in the channel
layer. The conductivity of the channel layer is modulated
through the doping/dedoping process, thereby achieving the
switching behavior of the device [1]. Studies have shown that
factors such as the type of electrolyte, ion concentration, and
the compatibility of the electrolyte‐semiconductor interface not
only influence the efficiency of ion transport, but also regulate
the coupling strength of ions and electrons. Consequently, these
factors play a crucial role in determining the properties of
devices, including switching speed, state retention, and synaptic
plasticity [24–26]. Therefore, the electrolyte is as important as
the channel layer, and its optimization and design are central to
improving performance of devices. Among various electrolyte
types, solid electrolytes offer significant advantages, such as
ease of integration [27], biocompatibility [2], and mechanical
stability [28], which improve the performance and application
potential of the devices. Additionally, Lee et al. [3] confirmed
that the type of anions in the electrolyte directly affects the
doping process in the channel layer, thus having an important
influence on the electrical and synaptic properties of OECTs.
Nevertheless, current research continues to confront several
challenges and unresolved issues. Notably, the interaction
mechanisms between the polymer semiconductors and an-
ions remain to be further explore. The mechanism of anion
and synaptic performance has not been fully elucidated, and
the effects of ion transport processes on conductivity, state
retention, and LTP/long‐term depression (LTD) behaviors
require additional investigation. Therefore, a systematic ex-
ploration of the impact of anions on the performance of
OECTs, especially their role in the modulating doping effi-
ciency and synaptic plasticity within the channel layer, is
essential. Such research will provide a critical theoretical
foundation
and
experimental
guidance
for
optimizing
devices, while laying the groundwork for the development of
high‐performance neuromorphic devices.
In this study, we aimed to elucidate the mechanism under-
lying the influence of anion type in solid electrolytes on the
performance of OECTs, with a particular focus on its regu-
latory effects on the electrical and synaptic properties of the
devices. For this purpose, we prepared solid electrolytes
using ultraviolet (UV)‐curing technology based on three dif-
ferent ionic liquids (ILs): EMIM TFSI, EMIM BF4, EMIM
OTf. By simulating various biological synaptic behaviors,
such as EPSC, STP and LTP, the effects of anions on the
synaptic plasticity were investigated. We integrated density
functional theory (DFT) calculations to unravel the interac-
tion
mechanisms
between
anions
and
polymer
semi-
conductors. The findings revealed that optimizing anion type
significantly enhances state retention, achieving a retention
time of approximately 1000 s and 64% of peak current, while
maintain
excellent
electrical
performance.
Furthermore,
based on the continuous ion doping and dedoping processes
of ions, we characterized the LTP/LTD performance, en-
abling linear modulation of conductance and an enhanced
of dynamic range. Building on these advancements, we
employed the Modified National Institute of Standards
and Technology (MNIST) database for handwritten digit
recognition, demonstrating that [TFSI]−OECT achieved a
high recognition accuracy of approximately 93%. These
results not only deepen the understanding of the anion‐
regulation mechanism but also pave the way for the optimi-
zation of high‐performance devices.

2.2
|
Preparation of Organic Semiconductor
Solutions
Using CF as the solvent, an appropriate amount of p(g2T‐TT)
powder was added to a sample bottle and stirred at 50°C for 4 h
to ensure complete dissolution. This process resulted in a
solution with a final concentration of 10 mg/mL.
2.3
|
Preparation of Electrolyte
M1, M2 and photoinitiator were mixed and heated at 80°C to
obtain the precursor solution for the electrolyte [29]. Subsequently,
the IL (EMIM TFSI) was added to the precursor solution at a mass
ratio of 3:1 (precursor solution to IL), followed by continuous
stirring at 80°C until a homogeneous mixture was achieved,
yielding the electrolyte solution. Subsequently, a liquid crystal cell
with a thickness of 100 μm was fabricated using two glass sub-
strates. The electrolyte solution was injected into the cell at 80°C
and then photo‐crosslinked under UV light for 10 min to obtain
the solid electrolytes. To prepare electrolytes with different anion
types, only the type of IL was varied, while all other preparation
parameters remained consistent.
2.4
|
Fabrication of OECTs
First, the channel layer of the OECTs was precisely patterned
using photolithography. Subsequently, a Cr/Au layer with a
thickness of 5 nm/50 nm was deposited by thermal evaporation
through a mask to form the source, drain, and side‐gate elec-
trodes. The channel length and width were 80 and 1600 μm,
respectively. Next, the p(g2T‐TT) solution was spin‐coated onto
the substrate at 2000 r/min for 60 s, followed by annealing at
60°C for 2 min. The electrolyte was then cut to an appropriate
size and laminated between the gate electrode and the channel
layer to fabricate the OECTs. A detailed fabrication process is
illustrated in Supporting Information S1: Figure S1.
2.5
|
Device Characterization
The structural analysis of the electrolyte materials was per-
formed using an X‐ray diffractometer (model: Bruker) with
diffraction angles ranging from 10° to 80°. Scanning electron
microscopy (SEM) (model: TESCAN) was employed to charac-
terize the microscopic surface morphology of the electrolytes.
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) of the electro-
lytes was conducted in a two‐electrode configuration using the
Lviumsoft software. The electrical performance and synaptic
properties of the OECTs were analyzed using a Keysight pre-
cision source/measure unit (B2912B) under inert gas conditions
within a glove box.
2.6
|
Computational Details
First‐principles calculations using DFT were carried out using
the Gaussian 16 program. Geometries were optimized using the
dispersion‐corrected B3LYP‐D3 functional with basis set of
6‐311G(d,p) for all atoms. Harmonic vibration frequency
calculations were performed for all stationary points to confirm
them as local minima (Nimag = 0). The structure of p(g2T‐TT)
was constructed with one monomer (n = 1) containing a total of
76 atoms.
2.7
|
Simulation of MNIST Based on Artificial
Neural Networks (ANNs)
Simulations of ANNs were performed on a Linux system using
the open‐source program “NeuroSim ver. 3.0” [30]. Specifically,
using 20 × 20‐pixel MNIST digital images as input, the black‐
and‐white patterns fed into the neural network in binary form.
The neural networks consisted of three layers: the input layer,
which included 400 neurons representing the 20 × 20‐pixel
MNIST digit images; the hidden layer with 250 neurons; and an
output layer with 10 neurons corresponding to the digits 0
through 9. During the simulation, it was necessary to consider
the basic parameters of the devices, including dynamic range,
nonlinearity (NL), and the number of conductance states. The
training process consisted 125 epochs.

Results and Discussion
3.1

Ionic Species‐Regulated Electrical
Characteristics of Solid‐Electrolyte‐Based OECTs
Synapses
Figure 1A illustrates a biological synapse and an artificial syn-
apse based on OECT. (The schematic diagram of the OECTs
mask layout is shown in Supporting Information S1: Figure S1).
In biological synapses, signal transmission is initiated by the
generation of action potentials in the presynaptic neuron upon
external stimulation. This triggers the release of neuro-
transmitters to the postsynaptic neuron, resulting in the gen-
eration of postsynaptic current (PSC) [31, 32]. Following these
basic principles, various biological synaptic behaviors (such as
STP, LTP, LTP/LTD) can be simulated by modulating synaptic
weights. The operational principle of OECTs is that the gate
voltage drives ions within the electrolyte to inject into the
channel layer to achieve electrochemical doping, thus mod-
ulating the drain‐to‐source current (Ids), which is similar to the
transmission process of biological synapses [1].
To investigate the compatibility between anions and the poly-
mer matrix, as well as their influence on synaptic properties,
three ILs featuring the same cation ([EMIM]+) but distinct
anions ([TFSI]−, [BF4]−, and [OTf]−) were utilized to fabricate
corresponding solid electrolytes. Due to their differences in
ionic radii and mobility, these anions can modulate their
interaction with the polymer matrix. In addition, the channel
layer was fabricated by spin‐coating (the detailed fabrication
process can be found in the Section 2 and Supporting Infor-
mation S1: Figure S2). The chemical structures of electrolytes
and polymer semiconductor are shown in Figure 1B.
To investigate the influence of anion types on the electrical
performance of OECTs, we measured the transfer curves of
various devices. The measurements were performed under the
following conditions: Vg = ± 4 V, Vds = −0.5 V, and scan rate

3.2

Effects of Ion Regulation on Nonvolatile
Synaptic Characteristics
The modulation of pulse amplitude, pulse width, and pulse
number is critical for tuning the performance of the devices
[3, 26]. Therefore, we investigated the synaptic properties of
OECTs using a pulse test system to clarify the influence of anion
type on synaptic properties (Figure 2 [3, 19–21, 23, 35–39]).
Figure 2A–C illustrates the single‐pulse tests with varying
amplitude for [TFSI]−, [BF4]−, and [OTf]−(Vg = −1 to −4 V),
where Vds = −0.5 V, and both the pulse width (tp) and pulse
interval (t) were set to 0.1 s. The results indicate that all devices
exhibit STP. With the increase in pulse amplitude, the electric
field strength is enhanced, accelerating ion mobility. This results
in a continuous increase in the peak EPSC (EPSCmax), which
reaches its maximum at the highest pulse amplitude, indicating
that the devices exhibit high state retention [40]. Moreover, we
evaluated the device performance by varying the pulse width
(tp ranging from 0.05 to 0.5 s) of a single pulse (Supporting
Information S1: Figure S10). The residual current was defined as
ΔPSC = EPSC5s −EPSCinitial [26], where EPSC5s represents the
EPSC measured 5 s after the pulse termination, and EPSCinitial
denotes the initial current before pulse application. The experi-
mental results show that, as the pulse width increases, the ex-
tended duration of electric field exposure allows a greater number
of anions to participate in the electrochemical doping process,
leading to a significant enhancement in ΔPSC for the devices.
To evaluate the LTP characteristics of the devices, we conducted
tests in which the number of pulses was increased from 10 to 300
(Figure 2D–F). Under these conditions, devices exhibited a con-
tinuous increase in EPSC, successfully achieving the transition
from STP to LTP. Notably, the [TFSI]−OECT demonstrated
superior LTP characteristics. Following the application of 300
consecutive pulses, the state retention of the different devices was

By comparing the performance metrics of various devices using
the radar plot (Figure 2H), it was found that the [TFSI]−OECT
exhibits superior state retention and excellent electrical per-
formance. Based on the analysis and calculation of the hyster-
esis windows, we found that the interaction between [TFSI]−
ion and the polymer semiconductor is stronger, which effec-
tively delays the reverse diffusion of ions into the electrolyte
and significantly enhances the nonvolatile memory retention of
the device. This study highlights the critical role of anions in the
doping and dedoping processes of the devices. Optimizing the
interaction between ions and polymer semiconductors, as well
as selecting ions that exhibit strong compatibility with the
polymer semiconductors, represents an effective strategy for
improving the state retention of the devices. The [TFSI]−OECT
demonstrated a retention time of approximately 1000 s and
maintained 64% of the peak current, which is significantly
superior to other OECTs (typically 20%–50%, Figure 2I,
Supporting Information S1: Table S3). This finding provides a
new direction for the development of high‐performance neu-
romorphic devices. In neuromorphic applications, the stability
of devices is as critical as state‐retention [41]. Therefore, we
evaluated the durability of the device through 5000‐pulse tests
(Supporting Information S1: Figure S13) [42, 43]. The results
showed that the [TFSI]−OECT exhibited a Gmax change of less
than 10%, demonstrating its excellent stability.

Mechanisms of Ion Dynamics:
Electrochemical and DFT Analysis
To investigate the correlation between the morphology of the
electrolytes and ion dynamics, this study analyzed the structure
of the solid electrolytes using techniques such as SEM, X‐ray
diffraction (XRD), optical microscopy, and electrochemical
analysis. The SEM results showed that the surfaces of all elec-
trolytes are relatively smooth (Supporting Information S1:
Figure S14A). Optical microscopy demonstrated that the surface
of the [TFSI]−electrolyte is relatively dense and uniform
(Supporting Information S1: Figure S14B), which may contrib-
ute to enhancing ion migration rates [44]. Additionally, XRD
analysis (Supporting Information S1: Figure S15) indicated that
all electrolytes exhibit a broad diffraction peak at 2θ = 20.81°,
indicating low crystallinity and an amorphous phase [45].

[BF4]−, and [OTf]−electrolytes, we conducted EIS measure-

Conclusion
This work presents a comprehensive investigation into the
modulation mechanisms of doping dynamics and synaptic per-
formance in OECTs through precise control of anion‐polymer
interactions. Specifically, we examined the interactions of three
distinct anions ([TFSI]−, [BF4]−, and [OTf]−) with the polymer
semiconductor (p(g2T‐TT)) and their influence on device per-
formance. Furthermore, we established a structure‐performance
relationship
model
based
on
“anion
characteristics‐anion
semiconductor interactions‐synaptic performance.” DFT calcu-
lations reveal that the state retention of the device is signifi-
cantly affected by both the composition of anions and their
interactions with the polymer semiconductors. The results
demonstrate that anion‐polymer interactions critically govern
synaptic characteristics. Specifically, the strong adsorption
between [TFSI]−and p(g2T‐TT) suppresses the dedoping
kinetics, resulting in improved retention time of [TFSI]−
OECTs. Therefore, [TFSI]−OECT exhibits the largest hysteresis
window (6.2 V) and the highest retention ratio (64%) within
1000 s, which are 2.1 and 2.3 times higher than those of [BF4]−
OECT (31%) and [OTf]−OECT (28%), respectively. These find-
ings further illustrate the advantage of [TFSI]−in enhancing the
state retention of devices. Furthermore, [TFSI]−OECT dem-
onstrated higher linearity, indicating its potential in artificial
synapses. Additionally, the recognition accuracy of 93% on the
MNIST dataset further demonstrates its potential for neuro-
morphic computing. This study not only elucidated the regula-
tory mechanism of anion type on the OECT performance but
also provided crucial theoretical insights for optimizing artificial
synaptic devices through electrolyte engineering, laying a
foundation for the development of high‐performance neuro-
morphic devices.
The electrolyte engineering strategy introduced in this study
provides a novel research direction for the development of high‐
performance artificial synapses. Future research may delve
deeper into the microscopic mechanisms of the interactions
between ions and polymer semiconductors, engineer a broader
range of solid electrolyte materials to optimize the performance
of devices, and enhance the recognition accuracy and stability
of neuromorphic devices. These efforts will lay the hardware
foundation for the development of efficient brain‐inspired
computing systems.

Abstract: Organic electrochemical transistors (OECTs) have garnered significant attention as artificial synapses due to their ability to emulate synaptic functionalities. While previous research has predominantly focused on modulating the physical properties of the channel materials to enhance synaptic performance, the role of ion dynamics in influencing device characteristics remains underexplored. Effective regulation of ion dynamics is crucial for improving state retention and achieving long‐term plasticity (LTP) in these devices. In this study, we propose a strategy to modulate the interactions between polymer semiconductors and ions in solid‐electrolyte‐based artificial synapses. Our findings indicate that the interplay between semiconductors and doping counterions significantly influences ion transport dynamics, thereby affecting the electrochemical doping and dedoping pro- cesses in OECTs. Notably, by suppressing the dedoping process, we achieved enhanced synaptic performances, with devices retaining 64% of the peak current after a retention time of 1000 s. Through the judicious selection of anions and optimization of their interactions with polymer semiconductors, we effectively controlled the dedoping process in OECTs, leading to improved state retention. These insights provide a novel perspective on tuning ion‐polymer semiconductor interactions for the development of high‐performance synaptic devices, advancing neuromorphic computing applications.
